The terminal matters

Confirm the ship, sailing date and actual terminal. Southampton or Dover alone is not a complete collection address.

02

Passenger readiness comes first

The ship’s arrival is the start of the transfer plan. Allow for disembarkation, luggage recovery and group assembly before the coach departure.

03

Protect the next connection

Plan airport arrivals or return-to-ship movements around their fixed deadlines. Optional visits need a clear fallback if the movement starts late.

BEFORE YOU REQUEST A QUOTE

01

Port, airport and hotel movements

UK Inbound Ground Transport handles Southampton and Dover group-transfer enquiries for tour operators, DMCs and cruise programme planners. Transport is operated by Evershine Transport Ltd. Share the ship, port, terminal where known, travel date and onward destination to begin a tailored quotation.

02

Disembarkation needs a realistic pickup window

The ship arrival time does not establish when the full group will be ready to board a coach. Explain the expected disembarkation arrangements, baggage collection and how the group will assemble. Confirm pickup instructions, the contact on the day and waiting terms in advance.

03

Airport connections need a full movement plan

For a transfer to Heathrow, Gatwick or another airport, provide flight times and the required airport arrival time. Include loading and road-journey allowances. Where passengers have different flights, identify the earliest critical departure and the terminal sequence before confirming the schedule.

04

Add sightseeing only when it fits

If you want a stop at Windsor, Stonehenge or another destination, include ticket times, luggage requirements and the final arrival deadline. Visits and meals must fit the available transfer window. Ask the written quote to specify whether attraction admission, parking and waiting time are included.

OPERATIONAL GUIDE · FOR TOUR OPERATORS & DMCS

Southampton Cruise Transfers: Plan Beyond the Berth

Build a dependable cruise movement around the ship, terminal, luggage, passenger release and onward connections.

Reviewed 15 November 2026 · UK Inbound Ground Transport

IN THIS GUIDE

Start with the sailing, then confirm the terminalBuild the collection around passenger readinessWork backwards from the next fixed commitmentTreat luggage as a vehicle requirementKeep sightseeing subordinate to the connectionThe brief to send before requesting a quote
Discuss your programme

A ship’s arrival time is the beginning of the transfer plan, not the coach departure time.

A cruise transfer may look simple on a sales itinerary: meet the guests in Southampton and continue to London, Heathrow or a regional hotel. The operational brief needs more detail. Passengers must leave the ship, recover their luggage, assemble together and reach an agreed collection point before the onward journey can begin.

Start with the sailing, then confirm the terminal

Record the ship’s full name, sailing date, cruise line and the terminal shown in the guests’ travel documents. Visit Southampton identifies five dedicated cruise terminals and directs passengers to their cruise booking confirmation for the departure terminal. Treat “Southampton docks” as an incomplete pickup address.

Ask the operating team to confirm the vehicle approach, access instructions and meeting arrangements for that specific call. Recheck changes close to travel. A familiar ship name is not a substitute for the actual booking details.

Build the collection around passenger readiness

Separate the published port arrival from the group’s expected release. Ask the cruise organiser how disembarkation is being managed and whether the guests will leave together. Agree who will count passengers, identify missing luggage and tell the transport team when the group is ready.

For a mixed group, record how split releases will be handled. Sending the coach away with only part of the party creates another movement; waiting for everyone can affect the onward schedule. Resolve that decision in the brief rather than at the kerb.

Work backwards from the next fixed commitment

An airport transfer has a different risk profile from an afternoon hotel arrival. Obtain the airline’s required airport arrival time and work backwards with the operator, including loading, traffic contingency and unloading. Do not promise a universal journey time or a guaranteed flight connection.

If the available window is tight, flag it before the programme is sold. An earlier flight may be unsuitable even when a car journey planner suggests the mileage is manageable. For embarkation, use the cruise line’s assigned arrival window and final boarding requirements rather than aiming at the ship’s sailing time.

Treat luggage as a vehicle requirement

Confirm the suitcase count, cabin bags, walking aids and oversized items. A group can fit the seats while exceeding the proposed luggage capacity. Ask for vehicle suitability to be confirmed against the actual brief and identify any accessibility requirements before allocation.

Keep sightseeing subordinate to the connection

A stop at Winchester, Windsor or another destination can enrich a private transfer, but it also adds unloading, walking, boarding and parking time. Agree an optional stop only after checking the core transfer. Record who can shorten or cancel it if the ship is late.

A shore excursion needs its own return-to-ship deadline and contingency. Do not reuse an airport-transfer schedule for guests who must rejoin a vessel.

The brief to send before requesting a quote

  • Ship, sailing date, confirmed terminal and travel direction.
  • Passenger numbers, luggage and accessibility needs.
  • Group release arrangements and a named representative.
  • Flight details or cruise boarding window, where relevant.
  • Any proposed visit, its priority and the fallback direct route.
  • Waiting terms, parking or access costs, and cancellation arrangements to confirm in writing.

Send UK Inbound Ground Transport the complete movement brief. The operating team can assess vehicle suitability and the proposed schedule before confirming availability and a quotation. A well-defined transfer gives the buyer a proposal that can be reviewed, rather than an attractive price built on missing assumptions.

OPERATIONAL GUIDE · FOR TOUR OPERATORS & DMCS

Scottish Highlands by Coach: Give the Landscape Time

Plan Highland touring around overnight locations, usable visiting time, coach access and a realistic daily rhythm.

Reviewed 15 November 2026 · UK Inbound Ground Transport

IN THIS GUIDE

Choose the overnight pattern firstMeasure the day in experiences as well as milesBuild a core route and an optional layerConfirm the practical welcomeProtect flexibility and driver feasibilityHighland programme review checklist
Discuss your programme

The best Highland itinerary leaves room for the place itself.

Edinburgh, Glencoe, Loch Ness and Inverness can make a compelling programme description. They are not, on their own, an operating plan. The quality of the journey depends on the sequence, the hotel locations and how much of each day remains after the coach has travelled.

Choose the overnight pattern first

Place the confirmed hotels on the route before adding visits. A hotel marketed under a destination name may be outside the centre or on a different side of the intended route. Use full addresses, not just town labels, and include access, unloading and overnight parking in the review.

Compare an overnight stay with a return excursion from an existing base. The right choice depends on the programme, but repeated out-and-back journeys can consume time that guests expected to spend exploring. One fewer hotel change may improve comfort; a better-positioned hotel may reduce driving. Make the trade-off explicit.

Measure the day in experiences as well as miles

Break each day into driving, comfort stops, visits, meals, boarding and hotel arrival. A photo stop still requires a safe place to stop, people to leave the coach and enough time to return. Several short stops can become a substantial part of the day.

Ask the operator to assess coach-suitable routes and realistic running times for the travel dates. Avoid using a car estimate as a passenger timetable. Give the guide a clear order of priorities so a late start does not turn every visit into a rush.

Build a core route and an optional layer

Separate the essential experiences from additions that depend on conditions and progress. For example, protect the main landscape visit and lunch window before adding another detour. This is a planning method, not a claim that a particular combination is feasible in one day.

VisitScotland’s trade itinerary resources are a useful starting point for destination ideas. Adapt those ideas to your group, vehicle, hotels and operating limits rather than treating an inspiration itinerary as an approved coach schedule.

Confirm the practical welcome

At every hotel and attraction, ask about group arrival procedures, coach approach, suitable parking and the walk from the drop-off. Record mobility requirements early. “Near the entrance” means little unless the actual stopping point and walking route have been checked.

Include the driver’s accommodation and meals in the written arrangements where required. A hotel booking for the passengers does not automatically include a suitable driver room or a place for the coach.

Protect flexibility and driver feasibility

Review daylight, seasonal opening arrangements, weather exposure and any date-specific access issues before committing to visits. Check the whole driver assignment with the operator, including positioning, genuine breaks, rest and evening movements. A free afternoon for passengers is not driver rest if the coach still has duties.

If the programme continues to Ireland, assess the journey to the departure port as a separate stage. Do not append a ferry to the end of an already full sightseeing day without reviewing check-in, loading and the onward movement.

Highland programme review checklist

  • Full hotel addresses in the intended overnight sequence.
  • Essential visits distinguished from optional stops.
  • Coach-suitable routing and realistic daily timings.
  • Meal, comfort and boarding allowances.
  • Verified access, parking and passenger walking distances.
  • Driver accommodation, evening duties and full schedule review.
  • A practical alternative if a visit or route becomes unavailable.

Share your proposed Scottish circuit with UK Inbound Ground Transport before fixing the final programme. A thoughtful route gives guests time to enjoy the Highlands and gives the operating team a schedule it can assess properly.

OPERATIONAL GUIDE · FOR TOUR OPERATORS & DMCS

Managing Heathrow Group Arrivals

Terminal coordination, luggage planning and a realistic first-day schedule for inbound groups arriving through Heathrow.

Reviewed 15 November 2026 · UK Inbound Ground Transport

IN THIS GUIDE

1. Plan the terminal and the collection procedure2. Landing time is not collection time3. Match the luggage to the vehicle4. Keep the first day flexiblePre-arrival checklist
Discuss your programme

A smooth arrival begins before the flight lands.

For an overseas tour operator or DMC, Heathrow is more than a collection point. It is where the programme meets immigration queues, baggage delivery, terminal access and the realities of moving a group together. A delay here can affect hotel check-in, attraction bookings and the driver’s remaining working day.

1. Plan the terminal and the collection procedure

Confirm the flight number and terminal, then agree a meeting point, representative contact and signage wording. Heathrow’s standard charter-coach collection procedure involves a parking/forecourt permit, reporting to West Ramp Coach Park and being dispatched by the marshal team. Out-of-hours arrangements differ; check the airport’s current instructions for the actual collection time.

Once everyone has cleared baggage reclaim and customs, the group representative should coordinate with the forecourt coach marshal. Follow the marshal’s directions about bringing passengers to the stand. Do not assume a telephone call to the driver alone authorises access. Terminal 5 may involve an additional forward holding area.

Buyer takeaway: Confirm who books the permit, who meets the group and who coordinates the call-forward. Include airport charges and agreed waiting terms in the quotation.

2. Landing time is not collection time

Build an arrival allowance around the group’s passport profile, baggage, mobility needs and size. For an initial programme draft, 60–90 minutes after landing may be a useful working allowance, with a longer contingency where appropriate. These are planning assumptions, not Heathrow service standards, minimum clearance times or guarantees. Some arrivals take substantially longer.

Keep flight monitoring separate from passenger readiness: an aircraft can be on stand while the group is still waiting for bags. Agree how delays, missing luggage and passengers arriving on different flights will be handled.

3. Match the luggage to the vehicle

A seat count does not establish luggage capacity. Specify the number and approximate size of suitcases, cabin bags, wheelchairs, walking aids and any oversized equipment. Ask the operating team to confirm the suitability of the allocated vehicle, especially for smaller executive groups with long-haul luggage.

4. Keep the first day flexible

Routing directly towards Windsor, Oxford, Bath or a regional overnight can avoid a journey into central London. It also creates a longer operational commitment if the flight is late. Driver checks and positioning already consume part of the day before passengers board; unloading, parking and finishing duties must also be included.

Prefer flexible sightseeing on arrival day. Before buying timed tickets, agree the latest workable departure from Heathrow and the alternative plan if it is missed. That might mean shortening a visit, travelling directly to the hotel or arranging additional transport, subject to availability and price.

Pre-arrival checklist

  • Flight number, terminal, travel date and scheduled arrival.
  • Passenger count, luggage and accessibility requirements.
  • Representative contact, meeting point and signage.
  • Permit arrangements, airport charges and waiting terms.
  • Onward route, driver feasibility and a delay contingency.

Share your arrival brief with UK Inbound Ground Transport so the operating team can review the movement, vehicle requirements and onward schedule before confirming a proposal.

A Better Coach Brief Makes a Better Quotation

A practical checklist for comparable coach proposals: movements, luggage, access, driver arrangements, inclusions and changes.

Reviewed 15 November 2026 · UK Inbound Ground Transport

IN THIS GUIDE

Describe every movementDescribe the group as well as its sizeMake hotel and driver arrangements explicitAsk for the assumptions behind the priceCompare scope before comparing totalsControl revisions with one current briefYour ready-to-send checklist
Discuss your programme

A useful quotation begins with a shared understanding of the job.

Two coach prices are difficult to compare when one assumes a direct transfer and the other includes sightseeing, evening movements and driver accommodation. The cheapest headline figure can simply reflect the shortest interpretation of an incomplete brief. Give each supplier the same operating picture before assessing the proposals.

Describe every movement

Send a dated, day-by-day schedule with pickup addresses, overnight hotels, visits, meal stops and the final drop-off. Include flight or ship details where relevant. Mark timings as fixed, preferred or provisional so the operator knows where the programme can flex.

Evening restaurant transfers, guide collections, shopping stops and hotel changes should be visible. “Coach at disposal” needs a defined service window and agreed scope; it should not stand in for a list of expected duties.

Describe the group as well as its size

State the passenger count and identify whether it includes the tour leader or guide. Add the number and approximate size of suitcases, cabin bags, mobility aids and unusual equipment. Request essential facilities explicitly and ask for suitability to be confirmed for the allocated vehicle.

A coach category or attractive fleet photograph does not establish the capacity or facilities of the vehicle available on your date. Where an accessibility feature is essential, settle that before booking.

Make hotel and driver arrangements explicit

Give full hotel addresses and flag access information already obtained from the property. Ask who arranges and pays for coach parking, driver accommodation and meals. Identify whether the driver is expected to provide any further movement after the group reaches the hotel.

For ferries or other crossings, agree who makes the booking, what is included and how changes will be managed. A line on an itinerary is not evidence that a crossing or suitable vehicle space has been reserved.

Ask for the assumptions behind the price

Request a written statement of inclusions and exclusions. Depending on the job, points to clarify include parking, airport or port access, road charges, ferries, driver expenses and additional waiting. Ask how VAT is treated in the actual proposal rather than applying a blanket assumption.

Confirm quotation validity, availability, deposit requirements, payment dates and cancellation terms before committing. An enquiry, draft itinerary or indicative price is not a confirmed transport booking.

Compare scope before comparing totals

Put proposals side by side against the same checklist. Check the vehicle commitment, service window, movements, luggage assumptions and responsibility for expenses. If an item is missing, ask for clarification rather than interpreting silence as inclusion.

Include supplier checks in the decision. Confirm the contracting business and request relevant operator licence and insurance evidence. Assess the proposed arrangements as a whole, including how feasibility issues and operational changes will be communicated.

Control revisions with one current brief

Give the programme a version number or issue date and highlight material changes. A new hotel, added visit or later evening finish can affect price, access and driver feasibility. Obtain written acceptance of the revised scope before treating the earlier price as applicable.

Keep one named buyer contact and one agreed operational contact path. Close to departure, reconcile the final itinerary, passenger numbers, meeting arrangements and emergency communication plan with the operating team.

Your ready-to-send checklist

  • Dates, group size and dated programme version.
  • Every movement, full addresses and timing priorities.
  • Luggage, accessibility and essential vehicle facilities.
  • Hotel access, coach parking and driver arrangements.
  • Crossings, waiting expectations and evening duties.
  • Requested inclusions, commercial terms and supplier evidence.
  • A named contact and a process for approving changes.

Send your brief to UK Inbound Ground Transport through the enquiry page. Clear inputs help the operating team identify missing details, review the route and prepare a proposal that your contracting and operations colleagues can assess.

London Emissions Zones & Central Coach Access

Understand vehicle compliance, legal stopping points and coach repositioning before confirming a London programme.

Reviewed 15 November 2026 · UK Inbound Ground Transport

IN THIS GUIDE

1. Distinguish LEZ from ULEZ2. Check Congestion Charge status separately3. Validate each collection and drop-off4. Budget for holding and repositioningLondon programme checklist
Discuss your programme

A London address is not a confirmed coach stopping point.

London programmes bring several separate decisions together: emissions compliance, charging status, street access and somewhere lawful to stop. Settling one does not settle the others. A modern coach may meet emissions standards and still be unable to collect outside a particular hotel.

1. Distinguish LEZ from ULEZ

Diesel buses, coaches and minibuses over 5 tonnes gross vehicle weight are subject to London’s Low Emission Zone (LEZ), with Euro VI the required emissions standard to avoid the applicable LEZ charge. These heavier passenger vehicles are outside ULEZ’s vehicle scope; they do not become ULEZ-compliant merely by meeting LEZ standards.

Minibuses up to and including 5 tonnes fall within ULEZ’s relevant vehicle category. The usual ULEZ standards are Euro 6 for diesel and Euro 4 for petrol. Older diesel minibuses may also be subject to LEZ requirements, so a simple “LEZ or ULEZ” distinction is insufficient.

LEZ operates daily throughout the year. ULEZ operates daily except Christmas Day. Check the actual registration with TfL, including any overseas-vehicle registration requirements, rather than relying on vehicle age or a fleet description. Ask for any applicable charge to be identified in the quotation.

2. Check Congestion Charge status separately

Emissions compliance does not establish Congestion Charge exemption. Vehicles with nine or more seats, including the driver, can qualify for a 100% discount. Vehicles recorded in the relevant bus taxation class may be automatically exempt; other eligible vehicles require an approved registration. The operating team should verify the specific vehicle’s status before travel.

Where an application is required, do not assume the discount applies while approval is pending. Recheck if the allocated vehicle changes.

3. Validate each collection and drop-off

Yellow lines, coach bays, red routes, bus stops and bus lanes have different restrictions. Boarding and alighting may be permitted at some locations, but signs, markings, time limits and local traffic orders govern the actual stop. A designated coach bay can have its own permitted waiting period; a general boarding allowance is not permission to park.

Red routes require particular care. Do not plan a stop on prohibited red lines. Some designated red-route bays allow coach boarding and alighting under their signed conditions. Likewise, do not assume a touring coach may use a local bus stop or every bus lane.

Buyer takeaway: Record a verified stopping point, passenger walking distance and accessible alternative for each hotel, attraction and restaurant. Check current roadworks and temporary restrictions near the travel date.

4. Budget for holding and repositioning

Ask the operator to identify suitable coach parking or holding arrangements between movements. Availability, opening hours, booking requirements and maximum stays must be confirmed. Do not treat Victoria Coach Station, a busy kerbside bay or a familiar street as an unrestricted waiting facility.

A coach may need to travel away after dropping the group and return later. Allow route-specific repositioning time and parking costs. The guide should assemble passengers at a safe agreed meeting point and coordinate with the driver before the vehicle approaches.

London programme checklist

  • Check LEZ, ULEZ and Congestion Charge status for the allocated registration.
  • Verify legal stopping points and walking distances.
  • Confirm coach parking, costs and repositioning time.
  • Check height, width, weight, bus-lane and timed access restrictions.
  • Agree direct guide–driver communication and a fallback meeting point.

Send your hotel list, sightseeing schedule and group profile to UK Inbound Ground Transport. The operating team can review vehicle suitability and proposed access arrangements before preparing a quotation.

OPERATIONAL GUIDE · FOR TOUR OPERATORS & DMCS

Planning Realistic UK & Ireland Coach Itineraries

How driving limits, overnight rest, weekly rest and ferry arrangements shape a workable multi-day coach programme.

Reviewed 15 November 2026 · UK Inbound Ground Transport

IN THIS GUIDE

1. Establish the applicable rules2. Build around driving limits3. Protect real breaks4. Include the whole working day5. Plan weekly rest across the complete assignment6. Treat ferry rest carefullyPre-sale validation checklist
Discuss your programme

A route can fit on a map and still fail in the driver’s schedule.

For tour operators and DMCs, transport feasibility needs checking before a programme goes on sale. A mileage total cannot show whether the driver has time for loading, daily checks, positioning, genuine breaks and overnight rest.

1. Establish the applicable rules

Commercial touring vehicles constructed to carry nine or more passengers in addition to the driver generally fall within assimilated drivers’ hours rules on journeys wholly within the UK. DVSA identifies AETR rules for international journeys. For UK–Ireland and wider European operations, have the operator establish the applicable regime for the full journey; do not assume every EU flexibility applies to a UK-operated international tour.

2. Build around driving limits

The core daily driving allowance is nine hours, extendable to ten hours twice in a fixed week. The limits are 56 driving hours in a week and 90 across two consecutive weeks. Daily driving is measured between qualifying rest periods, rather than being a fresh allowance at midnight.

Include empty positioning and local movements. A long first week reduces the capacity available in the next. Leave realistic traffic headroom and use coach-suitable routing, particularly in the Highlands, rural Ireland and congested urban areas.

3. Protect real breaks

After no more than four and a half hours of driving, the driver normally needs a 45-minute break. Under the standard split arrangement, at least 15 minutes must come before at least 30 minutes. The operator should confirm any journey-specific flexibility before using it.

A sightseeing stop does not automatically provide a break. Driving to the coach park is driving time; cleaning, refuelling and helping passengers are work. Plan a genuine duty-free window and identify where the coach can lawfully stand.

4. Include the whole working day

The usual single-driver planning framework requires 11 hours of daily rest within the relevant 24-hour period, or a permitted reduced rest of at least nine hours. No more than three reduced daily rests are allowed between weekly rests. A qualifying split regular daily rest follows a different structure and must be checked separately.

Daily-rest planning usually leaves a 13-hour spread, or up to 15 hours with permitted reduced rest. Count from the start of work, including checks, to the completion of all duties—not simply the passenger collection and hotel drop-off. Driving time, working time and the elapsed duty spread are different measures.

Example: An 08:00 duty start followed by work until 23:45 exceeds the ordinary 15-hour single-driver planning window. A later start the following morning does not repair that first day. Arrange a separate evening transfer or redesign the day before confirming the programme.

5. Plan weekly rest across the complete assignment

Normally, weekly rest must begin by the end of six consecutive 24-hour periods following the previous weekly rest. Regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours; a permitted reduction to at least 24 hours carries compensation requirements. Review consecutive weeks and the driver’s duties before and after your tour.

There is an important exception: qualifying international occasional passenger services can postpone weekly rest for up to 12 consecutive 24-hour periods, subject to conditions and subsequent rest requirements. This is not automatic permission for any 12-day itinerary. The operator must confirm eligibility, recording equipment, any night-driving conditions and the full rest plan. Daily driving, breaks and daily rest still matter.

Regular weekly rest must not be taken in the vehicle. Arrange suitable accommodation when required. A passenger “free day” only provides driver rest if the driver is genuinely released from work for the necessary continuous period.

6. Treat ferry rest carefully

Where the applicable ferry/train exception is satisfied, regular daily rest can be interrupted no more than twice, with interruptions totalling no more than one hour and the required sleeping facility available. The required actual rest must still be completed. There is no general rule adding two hours to make an 11-hour rest into 13 hours.

A ferry booking is not proof of a valid rest plan. Include port check-in, queues, loading and unloading; have the operator validate cabin availability, the rest taken before and after sailing and the applicable completion window. A short daytime crossing does not by itself provide a full daily rest.

Pre-sale validation checklist

  • Provide every hotel location, visit time, ferry and evening transfer.
  • Include depot movements, checks, loading, parking and finishing duties.
  • Identify genuine breaks and suitable overnight accommodation.
  • Validate daily, weekly and fortnightly limits against the driver’s wider roster.
  • Check working-time and night-work requirements as well as driving limits.
  • Agree a relief-driver, separate-transfer or itinerary-change contingency.

Working-time rules can constrain a programme even when driving limits are respected. For workers in scope, requirements include working-time breaks, an average weekly limit and night-work provisions. The operating team should assess them alongside the tachograph plan.

Send your day-by-day route, hotels and group profile to UK Inbound Ground Transport. We review proposed transport schedules with the operating team to identify feasibility issues before a quotation is confirmed.

Arrival-day planning, before the first visit

For a group arriving from China, share the flight number, terminal and whether everyone travels together. Schedule the first coach movement around immigration, baggage reclaim and group assembly. If London sightseeing, Windsor or another timed visit follows the arrival, identify what can move if passengers are ready later than planned. Agree the meeting arrangement and a tour-leader contact before travel.

02

Oxford, Cambridge and shopping stops

If your programme includes Oxford, Cambridge or Bicester Village, give each visit a realistic time allowance. Walking tours, shopping, meals and coach collection are separate parts of the movement. Set an agreed meeting time and place for the whole group, and confirm coach access and parking with the relevant venues. Shopping is an optional element of your brief, not an assumed requirement for every Chinese group.

03

Keep a multi-city route workable

A London–Oxford–regional England–Edinburgh outline can be a starting point for discussion, but it is not a confirmed daily schedule. Provide the number of nights and essential visits so routing, hotel positions and driver requirements can be reviewed together. Adding Scotland or Ireland changes the travel commitment; a longer destination list needs more time or fewer visits.

04

Group communication and multiple vehicles

Tell us the tour leader’s working language, contact details and how instructions will reach passengers. Any requested language support must be agreed separately; it is not automatically included. If more than one vehicle is needed, specify passenger allocation, separate arrival flights and whether each coach has a group representative. Availability and coordination arrangements are confirmed in the written proposal.

Travel dates and gateways; passengers and luggage; daily movements and timed visits; hotel addresses and driver-room arrangements; accessibility needs and essential vehicle features. Include your company, contact details and the tour leader’s details where known.

Request this in your brief. Vehicle continuity, driver duties, rest and availability need review across the complete programme before confirmation.

Shopping, evening duties and driver rooms

If Bicester Village or another shopping stop is requested, include the intended time on site and luggage implications. VEHICLE PLANNING · 16 NOVEMBER 2026

Coach Luggage Planning: Choose More Than a Seat Count

Thirty passengers do not describe the whole coach requirement. Their bags, equipment and daily movements matter just as much.

All operational guides →

FOR TOUR OPERATORS & DMCS

Practical questions for a clearer transport brief.

Discuss your programme →

Start with a luggage brief, not a vehicle label

A coach enquiry often begins with one number: the passenger count. That is essential, but it does not describe what has to fit in the luggage space. A group travelling with one compact bag each presents a different requirement from a group with large suitcases, cabin cases and extra equipment. Before selecting a vehicle, give the operator a realistic description of the load. Confirm suitability for the actual vehicle offered, rather than relying on a general fleet category or photograph.

Count everyone and everything travelling

Include paying guests, the tour leader, guides who will travel with the group, and any other accompanying staff. Record large suitcases, smaller cases and hand luggage separately. Identify wheelchairs, walking aids, pushchairs, sports equipment, musical instruments or oversized items. Where dimensions are important, provide them. A request for “room for luggage” leaves the supplier to guess; a counted list gives the operating team something it can assess.

Use a clear example without inventing an allowance

For example, a brief might read: “30 guests and one tour leader; 31 large suitcases and 31 small bags; two folding walking aids; no additional guide travelling between hotels.” This is a description of the proposed load, not a promise that it will fit a particular coach. Ask the operator to confirm the allocated vehicle’s seating, luggage arrangement and any access requirements against that brief. Reconfirm if passenger numbers or baggage change.

Distinguish a transfer from a touring day

An airport-to-hotel transfer carries the group’s main bags. A sightseeing day from the same hotel may carry a lighter load, while a day that changes hotels carries everything again. Mark each overnight move on the itinerary. If the group leaves luggage with a hotel, obtain the hotel’s agreement and record collection arrangements. Do not assume that bags can be left with a venue or that the driver can supervise items away from the vehicle.

Allow for what the group adds during the tour

Shopping stops, gifts, event materials and extra purchases can change the load after the first day. Ask the organiser whether the group expects significant additional baggage, especially before the final airport transfer. Explain any known changes when seeking the quotation. The practical answer may involve a different vehicle or another agreed arrangement; it should be confirmed before the group arrives, with the cost and responsibility clear.

Keep airport assembly and loading in the schedule

Counting bags is also a timing task. The group needs time to collect its luggage, assemble and reach the agreed collection point. Heathrow’s official group-coach guidance asks leaders to have passengers together and ready before requesting the coach. Build loading and passenger checks into the movement plan. A scheduled landing time should not be presented as a guaranteed coach departure time.

Confirm the essentials in writing

Ask the proposal to identify the passenger load, luggage assumptions, essential accessibility features and the movements included. Where a wheelchair-accessible vehicle is required, confirm the specific requirement and allocation before booking; luggage space and passenger accessibility are separate questions. Agree how changes will be communicated and reviewed. A complete brief makes it easier to compare quotations and reduces the risk of discovering an unsuitable assumption on arrival.

Your planning checklist

  • Passengers, tour-leader seats and any travelling guides.
  • Large suitcases, small cases, hand luggage and oversized items.
  • Mobility aids and essential passenger-access requirements.
  • Hotel-change days and any agreed luggage-storage arrangements.
  • Shopping or event items expected during the programme.
  • Written confirmation of suitability for the vehicle offered.

HOTEL & ROUTE PLANNING · 16 NOVEMBER 2026

Hotel Coach Access: The Detail That Can Disrupt a Group Tour

A hotel can suit the guests beautifully and still need a careful coach arrival plan. Check the last few hundred metres before the programme is confirmed.

All operational guides →

FOR TOUR OPERATORS & DMCS

Practical questions for a clearer transport brief.

Discuss your programme →

An address is the beginning of the access plan

A confirmed hotel booking does not establish where a coach can unload. A city-centre entrance, a courtyard approach or a narrow historic street can all affect the last part of the journey. Tour operators and DMCs should provide full hotel addresses at quotation stage and obtain practical access information from each property. Ask the transport operator to review that information against the proposed vehicle and daily route.

Ask the hotel precise questions

Can the intended coach reach the entrance? Where is the agreed unloading point, and is it suitable for the group’s arrival time? How far will guests walk with their bags? Are there steps or other access issues the organiser needs to know about? Ask the hotel to identify the correct vehicle entrance and any restrictions it knows about. A statement that “coaches visit regularly” is useful context, but the current arrangements still need confirmation.

Separate unloading from parking

A place to unload is not necessarily a place to wait or park overnight. After guests leave the vehicle, the coach may need to move elsewhere. Establish where it will go, whether a reservation is needed, who pays and how much repositioning time belongs in the day. For London movements, consult current Transport for London coach-driver resources and the relevant local authority or parking operator. A hotel’s advice does not replace the restrictions applying at the actual stopping point.

Make luggage and assistance arrangements practical

If the coach cannot unload at the entrance, describe the walking route and distance rather than leaving the group to discover it on arrival. Discuss any mobility requirements with the organiser and property. Confirm who will assist with bags where assistance is needed; porters and luggage handling should not be assumed to be included. Give the tour leader a clear arrival instruction that matches the transport plan.

A driver room does not remove the parking question

Where the itinerary requires driver accommodation, specify who books and pays for the room, which property it is in and how the driver reaches it after parking. Include any movement between the parking location and accommodation in the operating discussion. The operator must assess duties and rest across the complete programme. A room reservation alone does not confirm that the driver’s schedule is workable.

Include dinner and evening transfers from the start

A day may appear to end at hotel check-in, yet the organiser may also expect a restaurant transfer and a late collection. Put those duties in the original brief, with addresses and times. If the evening movement needs a separate vehicle or another arrangement, settle that before selling the final programme. It is much easier to review one complete schedule than to add late duties after a touring price has been agreed.

Plan the following morning as carefully as arrival

Specify the loading point, departure time and who will assemble the group. Allow time for room checkout, bags and boarding before a timed visit or airport movement. Check whether the morning pickup location differs from the arrival unloading point. Provide a hotel contact and an agreed alternative if access is disrupted, and make sure the group representative knows how the operating team will communicate changes.

Your planning checklist

  • Hotel name, full address and correct coach approach.
  • Agreed unloading and next-morning pickup points.
  • Walking distance, luggage assistance and passenger access needs.
  • Parking location, booking requirements, charges and responsibility.
  • Driver accommodation and any associated movements.
  • Restaurant transfers, evening duties and the following day’s first commitment.
